title: Dislocation recurrence rate and functional outcome in patients following traumatic anterior shoulder dislocation, depending on glenohumeral and osteochondral morphology, associated intra-articular injuries and surgical management
summary:
The shoulder joint is highly mobile due to its unique anatomy. However, this also means there is an increased risk of the shoulder dislocating following an accident. Various bony and soft-tissue factors play a role in the stability of the shoulder joint. These include, amongst other things, the shape and orientation of the glenoid cavity. In the event of a shoulder dislocation, changes or injuries to the bones may occur alongside soft-tissue injuries. These include, for example, injuries to the anterior rim of the glenoid cavity (Bankart fractures) or indentations on the humeral head (Hill-Sachs lesions). These injuries, as well as associated injuries, the anatomical characteristics of the stabilising factors and the treatment, can influence the risk of re-dislocation and the subsequent function of the shoulder. However, it is not yet fully understood which of these factors are particularly important for the subsequent course of the condition.
The study aims to investigate how the anatomical structure and injury-related changes to the shoulder, associated injuries, patient-related factors and treatment are linked to the subsequent treatment outcome. In particular, the study will examine which factors are associated with the occurrence of recurrent shoulder dislocation, as well as with pain, shoulder function, range of motion, muscle strength and quality of life.
One part of the study involves analysing existing data from adult patients who were treated at the BG Klinikum Duisburg for traumatic anterior shoulder instability. To this end, data from medical records and existing CT and MRI scans are being analysed retrospectively. The data collected includes, amongst other things, the shape and orientation of the glenoid cavity, traumatic changes such as Bankart fractures and Hill-Sachs lesions, associated injuries, patient-related factors and the treatment administered. In addition, clinical and functional outcomes are assessed using standardised questionnaires on shoulder function, pain, quality of life and the ability to participate in sport and work.
In another part of the study, patients with traumatic anterior shoulder instability are being prospectively examined. Shoulder function and quality of life are assessed using standardised questionnaires. In addition, clinical examinations are carried out, including measurements of range of motion and muscle strength in both shoulders. The examinations are conducted during the post-operative or post-traumatic recovery period over a period of 24 months.
The data collected will then be analysed to determine whether, and in what way, anatomical, injury-related, patient-related and treatment-related factors are associated with the subsequent course of the condition and the functional outcome. The findings are intended to contribute to a better understanding of the factors that influence the course of the condition following traumatic anterior shoulder instability.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
•    Patients with traumatic anteroinferior shoulder dislocation who have undergone surgical treatment involving a Bankart repair (soft-tissue or bony) or bony glenoid reconstruction (e.g. Latarjet, J-Span) ± concomitant procedures (e.g. remplissage, LBS tenodesis, rotator cuff repair, etc.) or conservative treatment
•    Written consent to participate in the study
Exclusion criteria:
•    Concomitant injuries to the same or other limbs, or multiple trauma, which could necessitate further surgical intervention or affect follow-up treatment
•    The presence of (hemi-)prostheses or traumatic dislocations of shoulder prostheses
•    Lack of pre-operative imaging
•    Incomplete documentation in the hospital’s internal information system
